source: Liu et al. (2023) Large Language Model for Multi-objective Evolutionary Optimization (MOEA/D-LLM, MOEA/D-LO)
finding: A zero-shot LLM (GPT-3.5 Turbo) used as the offspring operator inside decomposition-based MOEA/D roughly matches a GA operator on five real-world bi-objective problems. It does not clearly beat it.
numbers: Hypervolume RE21-RE25, MOEA/D-GA vs MOEA/D-LLM: RE21 0.781 vs 0.7936; RE22 0.7221 vs 0.6853; RE23 1.1491 vs 1.1561; RE24 1.1574 vs 1.153; RE25 1.0812 vs 1.0812. N=50, 10 parents in, 2 offspring out per call.
quote: the extensive online interactions between our MOEA framework and the LLM can be time-consuming and resource-intensive
limits: Only 5 bi-objective instances. No cost or wall-clock reported. Two wins, two losses, one tie.
agent_relevance: An LLM proposing designs is about as good as a plain crossover operator. So selection (S7) should be done by code on measured objectives, not trusted to the model.

source: Liu et al. (2023) MOEA/D-LO linear operator distilled from LLM behaviour
finding: The authors fit a cheap white-box linear operator to LLM outputs. It is competitive with classic MOEAs on ZDT and UF, so the LLM's value can be copied without online calls.
numbers: Regression on 14,000 prompt-response pairs. Win/loss/tie on HV vs NSGA-II 2/11/1, vs MOEA/D 3/9/2, vs MOEA/D-DE 7/5/2 (direction of the columns is ambiguous in the paper). UF1 IGD: Random 9.85e-2, Equal 8.25e-2, LO10 4.22e-2; input size 10 best. 30 runs, N=200/300.
limits: Summary rows lack a clear reference column. ZDT/UF are synthetic benchmarks, not engineering design.
agent_relevance: What the LLM adds in search may be a simple move (step toward better parents plus noise). Code can do that, so S3 and S7 can be partly mechanised.

source: Lumina (2026) LLM-driven GPU design space exploration and DSE benchmark
finding: Small open LLMs are weak at reasoning about design trade-offs out of the box. Human-written corrective rules raise accuracy a lot. An LLM-guided explorer with such rules beats black-box search by a large margin in samples.
numbers: Benchmark: 308 bottleneck, 127 perf/area, 30 tuning questions. Qwen-3 original to enhanced: bottleneck 0.73 to 0.80, perf/area 0.59 to 0.82, tuning 0.40 to 0.63. Phi-4: 0.70/0.42/0.30 to 0.76/0.61/0.48. Llama-3.1: 0.47/0.23/0.26 to 0.53/0.39/0.46. Search: 4.7M-point space, 1,000 samples: PHV 32.9% above ML baselines, 17.5x sample efficiency, 421 superior designs vs 24 for ACO.
quote: Lumina was the only methodology that successfully discovered six designs surpassing the reference point
limits: One workload (GPT-3 inference). Only three open models. No component ablation of the framework. Accuracy stays well below 1.0 after rules.
agent_relevance: A measured case where domain rules fed to the model beat blind search. Tuning accuracy is only 0.3 to 0.6, so the model should propose and code should rank (G5, G8).

source: Lumina (2026) LLMCompass 20-sample budget run
finding: With a tiny budget of 20 expensive simulations, only the LLM-guided method found designs that beat the A100 reference. All black-box methods found none.
numbers: Lumina: 6 designs beat the A100. Design A: 1.805x TTFT/Area, 1.770x TPOT/Area, 0.772 normalised area. Design B: 0.592 TTFT, 0.948 TPOT, 0.952 area. In the 1,000-sample study BO ranked 4th; GA and grid search failed.
limits: Simulation takes about a week end to end. Simulator accuracy within 10% is taken from prior work. Single workload.
agent_relevance: Supports G12: LLM priors matter most when each evaluation is expensive and the budget is small.

source: iDSE (2025) Navigating design space exploration in high-level synthesis using LLMs
finding: An LLM-aided explorer finds the HLS Pareto front with far fewer synthesis runs than NSGA-II, MOEA/D, ACO and a lattice method. Warm-start seeding and a reflection loop explain most of the gain.
numbers: 12 benchmarks, ADRS averaged over 5 runs. Abstract: 5.1x to 16.6x closer to the reference front than heuristics, up to 25.1x exploration efficiency, matches NSGA-II with 4.6% of its designs. Designs to reach target ADRS (Polybench/MachSuite/CHStone): NSGA-II 108 each, HGBO-DSE 8/9/74, iDSE 4/5/7. 12 initial samples, 3 generations, population 12.
quote: matching NSGA-II with only 4.6% of the explored designs
limits: Speedup figures are inconsistent between Table 2 and Appendix D.2. Reference fronts built by random sampling and BFS; only 3 small benchmarks explored exhaustively. LLM named for warm-start is DeepSeek-R1; the optimiser LLM is not clear. Too many seeds cause output truncation.
agent_relevance: A seed-then-refine pattern: a few LLM-chosen starts, then a reflection step on the last trajectory. Fits S3 generate, S4 test, S7 select.

source: iDSE (2025) ablation of pruning, reflection and warm start
finding: Pruning invalid designs, reflecting on the trajectory, and bottleneck analysis each add measurable value. LLM warm start also helps NSGA-II but not ACO.
numbers: Baseline 12.4% invalid designs. Pruning removed 89.9% of invalid designs. Trajectory reflection +20.5% effectiveness. Bottleneck analysis and refactoring a further +45.0%. Warm start for NSGA-II: 2.5x over random sampling, 1.8x over BS, 1.6x over LHS (text); table-derived 3.17x, 2.32x, 1.9x.
limits: Percent gains are defined in the paper's own terms. Single hardware platform (ZCU106). Text and table disagree on warm-start gains.
agent_relevance: Cheap code-side checks (prune invalid before evaluating) deliver much of the saving. Matches G2: revise from real output.

source: Xu et al. (2026) MPM-LLM4DSE: multimodal predictor plus LLM optimiser for HLS
finding: An LLM optimiser with a prompt that states how each pragma affects quality of results beats metaheuristics and an earlier LLM-metaheuristic method. Under equal time on large spaces it beats a GNN-driven search.
numbers: Average gain 39.90% over prior DSE methods. LLM4DSE(Qwen3) average ADRS improvement 46.07% over conventional metaheuristics and 21.39% over LLMMH. On spaces up to 7 million configs and equal time: 32.66% ADRS reduction vs GNN-DSE (heat-3d 30.78%, jacobi-2d 52.70%, seidel-2d 14.51%). Prompt-strategy comparison used GPT-3.5-turbo. Models: GPT-4o, Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking.
limits: API call latency makes runtime high. Equal-time comparison uses the authors' own timing. Only a handful of held-out applications.
agent_relevance: Domain impact notes in the prompt (what each knob does) are the lever. This is the S2 representation step feeding S3.

source: Xu et al. (2025) Intelligent4DSE ECoGNNs-LLMMHs: LLM inside metaheuristics
finding: Swapping the random moves of NSGA-II, SA and ACO for LLM-proposed moves cuts ADRS strongly. The size of the gain depends a lot on which LLM and which metaheuristic.
numbers: Abstract: ADRS improvement 87.47% over metaheuristics; 68.17% over GNN-DSE and 63.07% over IRONMAN-PRO. Table 10 average ADRS: SA 0.3182, NSGA-II 0.2405, ACO 0.2842; LLMGA deepseek-r1 0.1409, gpt-4o 0.1784, gpt-4.1 0.1404, o3-mini 0.1755; LLMSA 0.0808/0.1304/0.1635/0.1991; LLMACO 0.0339/0.0932/0.1326/0.1616. Runtime 132-213 s classic vs 347-839 s LLM variants. 5 benchmarks.
limits: Only 5 unseen benchmarks. 12 combinations, one run each in the table. LLM variants cost 2 to 6 times the wall-clock.
agent_relevance: Model choice matters more than the search skeleton (0.034 to 0.16 for the same ACO). Do not assume one model's gain transfers (G7).

source: Multi-agent LLM framework for DSE in autonomous driving systems (2025)
finding: A set of LLM agents (interpret, run simulator, read results, propose next design) finds Pareto points sooner than a genetic algorithm on a small CPU/sensor design space.
numbers: Space: 28 cores x 5 frequencies x 2 LiDAR rates = 280 points. Constraints: navigation time under 400 s, control rate above 1 Hz. In 15 iterations the LLM agent found 6 Pareto-front points; the GA found 0 (its first came at iteration 20). Models: Llama 3.1, DeepSeek-R1, Mistral-small3.1, Llama 4 Scout via Ollama and AutoGen.
quote: the LLM-based approach concentrates on design points with navigation time under 250 seconds
limits: One robotaxi case, one parking map. Only 3 parameters. Cost is a CPU proxy. Prompting ablations omitted. Search focused on fast designs, so front coverage is narrower than the GA's. Vector-retrieval memory was biased to irrelevant snippets, so a plain text log was used.
agent_relevance: An early win in a 280-point space that a script could enumerate. The LLM is mostly a prior over where to look, with a coverage cost. Enumerate in code when the space is small.

source: LLAMBO (2024) Large language models to enhance Bayesian optimization
finding: Putting an LLM into BO as warm-starter, surrogate and candidate sampler works best early with few observations. Uncertainty calibration is worse than a GP.
numbers: GPT-3.5. Bayesmark 25 tasks, 5 seeds, 25 trials; M=20 candidates. Surrogate with n=5,10,20,30 obs: best NRMSE and R2, but GPs best on calibration. Acceptance rate of proposed candidates: 91.60% full, 88.8% no context, 69.26% no instructions.
quote: LLAMBO performs effectively as an end-to-end pipeline, exhibiting sample-efficient search.
limits: Task counts inconsistent between sections. Regret and rank only in figures. Cost much higher than classic BO. Tied to GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Calibrated uncertainty comes from code (a GP); the LLM gives prior knowledge. Split roles as in section 1 of the schema.

source: Yang et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Optimizers (OPRO)
finding: An LLM can climb an objective by reading a history of scored attempts. It works on small problems and degrades as the problem grows. It is sensitive to meta-prompt wording and temperature.
numbers: TSP optimality gap n=10: 0.0% for all three LLMs vs NN 13.0%, FI 3.2%. n=50: gpt-4 11.0% (FI 9.8%), text-bison 219.8%, gpt-3.5-turbo 133.0%. Linear regression: 4-8 steps inside start region, about 50 steps (gpt-4 50.4 +/- 18.8) far outside. Prompt optimisation: GSM8K 80.2% vs 71.8%; BBH gains up to 50%; 200 steps, 8 candidates per step.
limits: Train accuracy 5-20% above test (overfit). Optimiser uses error cases poorly. Context limit on large instances.
agent_relevance: Score-history prompting is a cheap select step but fails with scale and weak models. Needs a held-out check (G3).

source: Liu et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Evolutionary Optimizers (LMEA)
finding: An LLM as crossover and mutation operator on TSP is near-optimal at 10-15 nodes and falls apart by 25. A temperature rule that raises temperature when stuck cuts the gap sharply.
numbers: GPT-3.5, pop 16, 250 generations, 5 instances per set. rue-15 gap 0.06% vs OPRO 5.23%; rue-20 3.94% vs 26.30%; rue-25 18.72% vs 53.59% (best heuristic 1.41%). Self-adaptation on rue-20: 3.94 vs 11.82 without. Optimum found in 19 of 20 instances at 10 and 15 nodes.
quote: LMEA performs competitively to traditional heuristics
limits: Beats heuristics only on tiny instances. A small run takes about half a day.
agent_relevance: Raising temperature only after K=20 non-improving rounds is a code-checked impasse trigger, consistent with G1.

source: Evaluating LLMs for material selection (2024)
finding: LLMs rate materials for multi-criteria scenarios well above experts and with too little spread. Prompt type changes agreement little.
numbers: 136 experts, 10,544 scores, 16 scenarios, 9 material classes. GPT-4, Mixtral, MechGPT. MAE (0-10 scale) all about 3: zero-shot 3.069, few-shot 3.207, parallel 3.045, CoT 3.374. Mean z vs experts: zero-shot 0.451, CoT 0.563, parallel 0.112. Rating SD: experts 3.346, GPT-4 2.486, Mixtral 2.488, MechGPT 2.933. Mixtral gave titanium 9 regardless of scenario (SD 0.250). CoT took 57 min vs 3 min for GPT-4; parallel cut prompts from 144 to 16.
quote: In general, models tend to score all materials well above experts
limits: Paper gives no correlations. Text and table disagree on one mean (3.155 vs 3.115). Expert scores are not ground truth.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G5 and G8: a model scoring trade-off options is inflated and blind to context. CoT did not help and cost 19x time (G11).

source: Abhyankar et al. (2026) LLEMA: evolutionary search with LLMs for multi-objective materials discovery (ICLR 2026)
finding: LLM plus chemistry rules, a surrogate oracle and success/failure memory beats generative and LLM-only baselines on 14 multi-objective materials tasks. Each piece matters.
numbers: Hit rate (4 tasks, 250 iterations): plain LLM 4.4, LLM with memory 15.1, mutation+crossover islands 29.8, LLEMA 30.2; stability 1.8, 20.1, 21.5, 27.6; memorisation rate 95.3, 58.3, 25.3, 16.6 percent. Wide-bandgap hit rate: LLEMA-GPT 33.62, LLEMA-Mistral 17.08, diffusion baselines under 1. Cost: 563 input tokens per call, 15.84 s/iter vs base LLM 4.12 s.
limits: Properties are surrogate-predicted; DFT check on only 150 samples. Two mid-size models. Rule set is hand-written chemistry. Some baselines (End2end) beat LLEMA on single tasks, e.g. photovoltaics H.R. 24.59 vs 20.47-22.90.
agent_relevance: The plain LLM recalled known answers 95% of the time. Fresh candidates need external constraints and a code filter, not model judgement (G8).

source: Abhyankar et al. (2026) LLEMA model scale and efficiency appendix
finding: Hit rate climbs with model size from 7B to 14B and 32B; the authors read size as a proxy for domain knowledge. Extra compute per iteration is modest.
numbers: Qwen2.5 hit rates: High-k 4.46 / 10.20 / 13.27 for 7B/14B/32B; SAW/BAW 1.30 / 22.55 / 20.00. LLEMA about 1.5x tokens per iteration vs base LLM with 8-10x discovery quality. 3 API calls per iteration.
limits: Single-run table; non-monotone for 32B on SAW/BAW. Efficiency claim is on four tasks.
agent_relevance: G12: search needs a foothold. A 7B model had hit rates of 1-10%, 14B+ much more.

source: AutoCircuit (2026, ICML) Agentic Pareto front exploration for analog circuit designs
finding: An LLM orchestrator that calls ML tools explores the Pareto front better than LLM alone. A chosen subset of tools beat the full tool set.
numbers: Log-hypervolume up to 2.4x over LLM-only baseline. Two-stage op-amp in SKY130. Best config NSGA-II + g_m/I_d beat the full toolset. Fixed wall-clock budget.
limits: Abstract only read; no LLM name, budget length or other baseline numbers seen.
agent_relevance: More tools is not better: the schema should offer few operators and let code pick (section 4b).

source: Multidisciplinary design and optimization agent driven by LLMs (2025)
finding: An agent turns a natural-language brief into parametric CAD and FEA loops, with retrieval for concept variants, on three cases.
numbers: Cases: gas-turbine blade, machine-tool column, fractal heat sink. No quantitative result in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Three cases, no Pareto metrics, preprint.
agent_relevance: Shows the tool loop shape (generate, simulate, read output, revise) but no measured benefit; do not cite as evidence of gain.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Evolution of Heuristics (EoH)
finding: Evolving natural-language heuristic ideas plus code beats hand-made heuristics and FunSearch on three combinatorial problems at low LLM query budgets.
numbers: No figures read; the abstract says it beats FunSearch and hand-crafted online bin packing heuristics at low query budget.
limits: Abstract page only.
agent_relevance: Pointer for a later pass: idea-level search before code-level search.

source: e-SimFT (2025) Alignment of generative models with simulation feedback for Pareto-front design exploration
finding: Fine-tuning a transformer gear-train generator with simulator feedback and epsilon-style preference sampling widens the Pareto front over other multi-objective alignment methods.
numbers: Hypervolume N=30, 2 / 3 requirements: baseline 0.573 / 0.403; Rewarded Soup 0.560 / 0.403; Rewards-in-Context 0.580 / 0.427; SimFT 0.582 / 0.463; eps-sampling 0.603 / 0.454; e-SimFT 0.621 / 0.473. N=300: 0.692/0.537 baseline to 0.729/0.610. Cost hit rate 52.8% to 66.9%, bounding-box volume 49.4% to 62.3%. 30 test problems x 10 trade-off scenarios; |D|=7360.
quote: e-SimFT outperformed latest multi-objective alignment methods in terms of the hypervolumes of the Pareto fronts generated.
limits: Not an LLM; one generator and dataset. SD about 0.2 vs gaps of 0.02-0.05, so most gaps are inside noise. DPO can lower valid-design rate. Binary PPO reward did worse.
agent_relevance: Training-side work; for our no-training agent it only says that simulator rewards, not model opinions, drive the gain.

source: Cross-paper synthesis of c01, c03, c05, c07, c08, c09: where the LLM gain over blind search appears
finding: The gain over blind search shows in low-budget, expensive-evaluation settings with domain rules or impact notes in the prompt. It is absent or inside noise on synthetic multi-objective benchmarks (c01).
numbers: Reported gains: 32.66% to 87.47% ADRS reduction (HLS), 17.5x sample efficiency (GPU), 6 vs 0 Pareto points in 15 iterations (driving). On RE21-RE25 hypervolume: 2 LLM wins, 2 GA wins, 1 tie (c01).
limits: All wins are author-run against baselines run by the same authors, often with metaheuristics at default settings. No independent replication found in the sources read. Wall-clock cost is 2-6x higher in c08.
agent_relevance: Use the LLM as a prior only where each trial is costly and the first batch matters. Otherwise enumerate or run a cheap code search.

source: Xu et al. (2025) Intelligent4DSE: metaheuristic weakness on large spaces
finding: Classic metaheuristics fail on large HLS spaces (ADRS above 0.5 on mvt), while LLM variants reach about 0.15 to 0.45 there. Fine-tuning LLMs for DSE is judged too costly.
numbers: mvt ADRS: SA 0.5620, NSGA-II 0.5557, ACO 0.5138; LLMACO deepseek-r1 0.1516; LLMSA deepseek-r1 0.1668; LLMACO gpt-4o 0.4297. One-hour limit per benchmark. Sample schedule: (0.00005S,30) for S above 1e7 down to (0.5S,10) for S at most 500.
limits: Per-benchmark, single-run values; wide spread across LLMs.
agent_relevance: Large model-to-model spread: a selection rule should not depend on one model's single run.

source: Lumina (2026) failure modes of LLM reasoning in DSE
finding: Authors list the specific ways models misjudge trade-offs: picking changes that touch many resources at once, ignoring under-used units, computing deltas against a zero baseline.
numbers: Even after rules, perf/area accuracy tops at 0.82 (Qwen-3) and 0.39 (Llama-3.1); tuning 0.63 and 0.46.
limits: Failure list is qualitative.
agent_relevance: These can become code checks at S4 test on a proposed change (one knob at a time, never a zero baseline).

source: OPRO (2023) sensitivity and overfitting findings
finding: Results depend on meta-prompt order, score display and temperature. Low temperature stalls, high temperature weakens exploitation. Training accuracy exceeds test by 5-20%.
numbers: Defaults: 8 candidates per step, 200 steps, top 20 kept. BBH: optimised instruction beat the step-by-step prompt by over 5% on 19 of 23 tasks (PaLM 2-L scorer), 15 of 23 with text-bison.
limits: Prompt optimisation, not design-space search; uses 20% of each BBH task for tuning.
agent_relevance: Anything tuned on a set needs a held-out set (G3); a select step must be tested on items not used to pick it.

source: LLAMBO (2024) ablation: instructions matter more than context
finding: Removing task instructions from the prompt hurts candidate acceptance much more than removing problem context.
numbers: Acceptance 91.60 +/- 0.45% full; 88.8 +/- 0.39% without context; 69.26 +/- 0.79% without instructions.
limits: Acceptance rate measures whether proposals pass the paper's own validity criterion, not final optimum quality.
agent_relevance: A clear operator statement matters; consistent with fixed operator slots O1-O8.

source: Lumina (2026) baseline behaviour: GA, BO, ACO under a low budget
finding: Classical baselines do poorly in this low-budget setting: GA and grid search failed, BO ranked 4th, and ACO had high run-to-run variance.
numbers: ACO found 24 superior designs in 1,000 samples vs Lumina 421. ACO best-to-worst normalised PHV ratio 1.82x.
limits: Baselines may be weakly tuned; no independent tuning report.
agent_relevance: When citing LLM gains, baseline strength is untested; plan our own equal-token tests (G7).

source: Metrics used across the opened LLM design-search papers
finding: Every LLM paper above scores against NSGA-II, MOEA/D or ACO baselines with code-computed Pareto measures. None scores trade-off quality by model opinion.
numbers: Metrics seen: HV (c01, c19), IGD (c02), ADRS (c05, c07, c08, c21), PHV (c03), log-hypervolume (c16).
limits: Deb's NSGA-II paper and Papalambros's text were not opened in this pass; this line records only what the opened LLM papers use.
agent_relevance: For S7 select: use a Pareto filter plus a hypervolume or knee-point rule in code over measured objectives.
